title: Reactivity of Shale to Supercritical CO₂: Insights from SEM-EDS and Mineral Phase Evolution in Caney Shales for CCUS Applications
content: Understanding mineral–fluid interactions in shale under supercritical CO₂ (scCO₂) conditions is relevant for assessing long-term geochemical containment. This study characterizes mineralogical transformations and elemental redistribution in five Caney Shale samples serving as proxies for reservoir (R1, R2, R3) and caprock (D1, D2) facies, subjected to 30-day static exposure to pure scCO₂ at 60 °C and 100 bars (2500 psi), with no brine or impurities introduced. SEM-EDS analyses were conducted before and after exposure, with mineral phases classified into silicates, carbonates, sulfides, and organic matter. Initial compositions were dominated by quartz (38–47 wt%), illite (16–23 wt%), carbonates (12–18 wt%), and organic matter (8–11 wt%). Post-exposure, carbonate loss ranged from 15–40% in reservoir samples and up to 20% in caprock samples. Illite and K-feldspar showed depletion of Fe²⁺, Mg²⁺, and K⁺ at grain edges and cleavages, while pyrite underwent oxidation with Fe redistribution. Organic matter exhibited scCO₂-induced surface alteration and apparent sorption effects, most pronounced in R2 and R3. Elemental mapping revealed Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺, and Si⁴⁺ mobilization near reactive interfaces, though no secondary mineral precipitates formed. Reservoir samples developed localized porosity, whereas caprock samples retained more structural clay integrity. Results advance understanding of mineral reactivity and elemental fluxes in shale-based CO₂ sequestration.
